[[Category:Machine learning]]
[[Category:Large language models]]


The '''language model loss''' measures how "surprised" a [[large language model (LLM)]] is by the true values of tokens it attempts to predict.

== Formal definition ==

With [[model parameters]] $\theta$, the '''language model loss''' on training sample $\vec x=(x_1,\cdots,x_T)$:

$$
L(\theta)
=
-\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log_b P_\theta(x_t \mid x_{1:t-1})
$$

<blockquote>
$\vec x=(x_1,\cdots,x_T)$ is a text [[token]] sequence of length $T$ (e.g., <code>('I','am','myself','.')</code>).
</blockquote>

=== Unit ===

The unit of the language model loss is determined by $b$.

{| class="wikitable"
|-
! $b$
! Unit
|-
| 2
| Bit
|-
| e
| Nat
|-
| 10
| Hartley
|}

<blockquote>
Training reports conventionally quote $L_{\text{nat}}$.
</blockquote>

== Perplexity ==

Perplexity is the exponential of the loss in nats,

$$
\operatorname{PP}(\theta) = \exp\big(L_{\text{nat}}(\theta)\big),
$$

and reads as the effective number of equally likely tokens the model is choosing between. A loss of $1$ nat per token therefore corresponds to a perplexity of $e \approx 2.718$.

== Irreducible loss ==

The loss is bounded below by the [[conditional entropy]] of the text itself, since no model predicts next tokens better than the true distribution generates them.

== Loss and compute ==

It is empirically determined

$$
L(C) \propto C^{-\alpha},
\qquad \alpha \approx 0.05.
$$

The exponent governs how expensive further improvement is: halving the loss requires roughly $10^{6}$ times more compute, which is why the gap between $2$ nats per token and $1$ nat per token, a perplexity fall from $7.389$ to $2.718$, is very large in practice.<ref>{{#cite:Q3141}}</ref>
